strengths: Addresses an important problem: imputing missing sensitive attributes can conceal discrimination and undermine fairness interventions in graph learning.
Training the imputer to cooperate with the sensitive-attribute adversary is a plausible and potentially useful extension of existing fair GNN approaches.
Reports meaningful improvements on several benchmarks. On BAIL with GCN, BFtS achieves AVPR 0.88 and an equality-of-opportunity gap of 1.70%, compared with FairGNN’s 0.83 and 4.10%.

Evaluation includes four real datasets, synthetic graphs with varying assortativity, GCN and GAT backbones, ten runs, and sensitivity studies. Training pseudocode and an implementation link are provided.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees do not cover the actual training objective. Equations 7–8 omit the classification and imputation losses used in Equations 4–6, so minimizing the full classifier objective need not produce zero Jensen–Shannon divergence. Replacing optimization over a regularized, parametric imputer with an unrestricted supremum over sensitive assignments also requires explicit feasibility and realizability assumptions.

The convergence argument in Appendix 5.3 contains substantive mathematical errors. Distributions with disjoint supports have maximal Jensen–Shannon divergence, not zero. An entirely constant sensitive assignment makes one conditional distribution undefined. Furthermore, Corollary 1 only compares divergence values; it does not establish improved gradients or convergence. Final predictive performance does not validate this central theoretical claim.

The reported evaluation contains an impossible metric value: Figure 3(a) plots an RNF result near −2 for 1−ΔDP, although Equation 9 requires this quantity to lie in [0,1]. This needs correction and verification of the metric implementation. Table 1’s caption also incorrectly claims superior NBA accuracy over all baselines: vanilla has higher AVPR and F1.

The experiments do not isolate the main methodological contribution. BFtS changes both adversarial imputation and the classification loss, and Section 3.5 explicitly attributes BAIL accuracy gains to LDAM. Table 3 varies LDAM placement but does not remove adversarial imputation. A β=0 comparison with otherwise identical training, LDAM-equipped baselines, and comparable tuning budgets is needed to establish the contribution beyond FairGNN.

The missingness experiments do not adequately test the motivating concern of biased data collection. Varying the observed fraction from 20% to 50% does not establish robustness when missingness depends on sensitive group, label, or graph position; the masking mechanism is insufficiently specified. Direct comparisons between fairness estimated from imputations and fairness measured using true attributes would also substantiate the claimed underestimation mechanism better than representation visualizations.

Important implementation and evaluation details remain unclear. Equation 3 conditions on binary imputed groups, but the manuscript does not explain how gradients propagate through these assignments to train the imputer. Validation/test splits, optimizer settings, selected per-dataset hyperparameters, and the meaning of reported uncertainty values are also insufficiently documented. The code link is helpful, but the manuscript alone does not provide a reproducible specification.
